# How people decide what to buy lies in the ‘messy middle’ of the purchase journey
### Applying behavioral sciences principles to the purchase decision process
We conducted literary reviews, shopping observation studies, search trend analyses, and a large-scale experiment. Our aim was to understand how consumers make decisions in an online environment of abundant choice and limitless information. What we found was that people deal with scale and complexity by using cognitive biases encoded deep in their psychology.
### Cognitive biases that influence purchase decision-making
These biases formed the basis for our large-scale shopping experiment with real in-market shoppers simulating 310,000 purchase scenarios across financial services, consumer packaged goods, retail, travel, and utilities.
In the experiment, shoppers were asked to pick their first and second favorite brands within a category, and then a range of biases were applied to see if people would switch their preference from one brand to another. To test an extreme scenario, the experiments also included a fictional brand in each category, to which shoppers had zero prior exposure.
The results showed that even the least effective challenger, a fictional cereal brand, still managed to win 28% of shopper preference from the established favorite when it was “supercharged” with benefits, including five-star reviews and an offer of 20% extra for free. And in the most extreme case, a fictional car insurer won 87% share of consumer preference when supercharged with advantages across all six biases.
The experiment showed that, when applied intelligently and responsibly, behavioral science principles — and the behavioral and informational needs they align with — are powerful tools for winning and defending consumer preference in the messy middle.

Just came across a very interesting simulation study: What happens if you make AI agents simulate the behavior of typical shoppers – and then test marketing campaigns on them before launching anything in the real world? Researchers built a tiny virtual town and populated it with AI agents. Just 11 agents and 10 locations. Each agent had: • a budget • an energy level • food and shopping needs • memory • social connections • its own persona Then DeepSeek-V3 generated their plans, conversations, and purchase decisions.

So the agents went to work, ate, talked to each other, remembered things, invited friends somewhere – and independently decided where to spend money. The actual experiment was very simple: One fried chicken shop offered a 20% discount in the middle of the week. The researchers then watched what happened. • The shop’s revenue increased by 51% from Day 2 to Day 3 – even after (!) the discount. • Its market share grew from 30% on Day 1 to 41% on Day 3. • But the TOTAL market didn’t really grow.

So the discount didn’t create much new demand – it mostly pulled customers away from a competitor. • The local diner lost market share and saw revenue fall by 7%.

So in theory, systems like this could let marketers test: • discounts • promotions • price changes • new product launches • competitive scenarios on synthetic consumers before going into the real market.

AI can help a team build a new product feature in hours. Finding out whether people actually want it can still take weeks. Vectorial is betting that human behavior models can narrow that gap, and has raised $3 million in...
What the Accuracy Claims Measure Vectorial says it has modeled more than 2.5 million people and completed over 30,000 simulations. Its funding announcement reports that simulations have reproduced earlier user-study findings with more than 85% accuracy and describes SAPIENS as 30% more accurate at predicting behavior than general-purpose language models. Those are company-reported results. Its current website separately gives an 87% accuracy figure for held-out studies and a 35% improvement for matching real opinions. The company explicitly distinguishes opinion matching from behavioral accuracy. These figures should therefore be read as results for different evaluations, rather than a single interchangeable measure of how well software predicts people. For prospective customers, the useful test is how the model performs on their audience, their product, and decisions with known outcomes. A simulation that ranks two messages correctly is answering a different question from one that predicts the exact percentage of users who will buy. Vectorial itself acknowledges weaker performance for precise predictions in categories with limited behavioral data. This is also where simulated research differs from AI tools that automate market-research workflows. Faster survey preparation and analysis can improve the process of gathering human evidence. A behavior simulator instead generates predictions from a model, making calibration and validation central to the value of its output. From Research Expertise to Product Decisions

# Synthetic Shopper Simulation
...
AI agents acting as shoppers browse or judge a control and one or more variants, and the tool predicts which version would perform better. Some tools drive real browsers on live or staged pages, others compare screenshots. It is a way to pre-screen ideas, not a substitute for a live experiment.

## When to reach for it

Pre-screen a test backlog and drop the weakest variants before spending traffic.
Sanity-check a variant for obvious friction before launch.
Compare two themes or page versions when traffic is too low to test both live.

Often paired with A/B Testing.

### Pros

Returns a prediction in hours rather than weeks of live traffic.

Session replays and agent reasoning can surface friction worth investigating.

Useful for ordering a backlog when traffic is the constraint.

### Cons

Independent studies of predicting A/B winners land well below vendor headlines, and one study of 330 CRO tests found model judges close to chance.

Predicted effect sizes are often shrunk or inflated, so they cannot feed revenue forecasts or sample size planning.

Headline match rates can mislead, because many 'winners' in test archives come from non-significant tests.

Agents don't behave like real shoppers with real money, time pressure and habits.

## Practical considerations: sample sizes, tools, logistics
...
### Pair it

Anything worth shipping still goes through an A/B Test. Use synthetic results to decide what to test, never what to ship.

### Tool scope

Shopify SimGym compares two themes only, and bot protection can block its shoppers. Squoosh and VWO's synthetic test suit backlog screening better.

### Vendor claims

Ask how a match rate was measured, how many tests it covers and whether non-significant tests count as winners.

This is the item that most simulation pitches leave out. The problem they solve is real: a small B2B page cannot gather enough visitors. But the answer does not have to be fake visitors. It can be a better use of the real ones.

Here is my arithmetic, using the sample rule in Kohavi and colleagues' 2009 guide. A demo page converting at 3% needs about 12,933 visitors per variant to detect a 20% relative lift. At 3,000 visitors a month split two ways, that is about 8.6 months. Halve the variance and it is about 4.3 months.

Model predictions can help real tests by filtering out weak ideas before they take a test slot, or by serving as a variable that reduces variance. That is the honest role for simulated users today: a screen in front of a real test, not a replacement for it.

"Controlled experiments embody the best scientific design for establishing a causal relationship between changes and their influence on user-observable behavior," Ron Kohavi and his Microsoft co-authors wrote in Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery.

deepseek.snippet:
MarketMirror runs ads, prices and surveys past simulated buyers before anyone spends money. This week we went back through 4,501 survey answers saved from 13 of our own test runs, all for an invented fitness app called Fitloop, to see how simulated buyers actually answer. We made no new model calls. Every number below comes from simulated people, not real buyers.

## Simulated buyers rarely commit

Asked whether they would start a free trial, 1.6% said yes, 58% said maybe and 40% said no. Most answers came with a condition attached: show me the price, show me a workout first, prove you won't charge my card.

## Three panels, three verdicts

One of those runs had 3,000 people in three panels of 1,000. Claude wrote, interviewed and played one panel, Gemini another, Codex the third. All three got the same brief, the same questions and the same countries (India, the Philippines and Kenya in the same numbers). They are different people, because each model wrote its own.

The verdicts were far apart. In the Claude and Gemini panels, 23% and 29% said no. In the Codex panel, 94% said no, in every country.

## The reasons were close

Each answer also came with a sentence in the person's own words, which we score on a 1-5 purchase-intent scale by comparing it with anchor sentences. On that scale the panels averaged 3.05, 3.04 and 2.56. That's a gap of half a point.

The labels meant the same thing in every panel: a "no" averaged about 2.5 to 2.6 and a "maybe" about 3.2, whichever model wrote it. The Codex people weren't using "no" differently. They were a little less keen.

Each panel's answers were packed tightly, with a standard deviation of 0.3 to 0.5 on that 1-5 scale. Almost everyone sat near the line between maybe and no, so moving the whole panel down by half a point moved most of it across the line.

Image from a 3D simulation of a grocery store used in an experiment conducted by Ricardo Daziano, associate professor of civil and environmental engineering, to gauge New York City residents' perceptions of social distancing.

Ricardo Daziano, associate professor of civil and environmental engineering, is principal investigator on a one-year, $102,700 RAPID grant from the National Science Foundation to use immersive virtual reality (VR) to continue assessing New Yorkers' perceptions of social distancing as the COVID-19 pandemic evolves.

"We want to understand how people are making decisions based on compliance with the health guidelines," Daziano said. "Until a vaccine is developed, policymakers need to not only find the best incentives for people to avoid physical proximity, they also need to create plans for relaxing social distancing in the future. The behavioral forecasts from the models developed in this project will help guide those decisions."

In the next wave of experiments, participants will experience social distancing scenarios using head-mounted VR displays. The researchers will then construct mathematical models to analyze how people with varied backgrounds and political affiliations change their behavior in response to health threats.

The VR simulations will be designed and implemented by So-Yeon Yoon, associate professor of design and environmental analysis in the College of Human Ecology, and co-principal investigator on the grant. With recent advances in autonomous agents, the future of e-commerce could see human buyers take a back seat, letting AI agents browse, evaluate, and click "buy" on their behalf.

A[new paper](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5381574) by[Omar Besbes](https://business.columbia.edu/faculty/people/omar-besbes), Vikram S. ###### Abstract

Recent advances in the development of large language models are rapidly changing how online applications function. LLM-based search tools, for instance, offer a natural language interface that can accommodate complex queries and provide detailed, direct responses. At the same time, there have been concerns about the veracity of the information provided by LLM-based tools due to potential mistakes or fabrications that can arise in algorithmically generated text. keenable.snippet:
**Short answer:** Not yet. The best published result, Shopify's [SimGym preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.19219), matched the direction of real add-to-cart shifts in 77% of 50 shops, but the size of the effect correlated only at 0.55. keenable.title: Online Controlled Experiments for Personalised e-Commerce Strategies: Design, Challenges, and Pitfalls
keenable.snippet: Online controlled experiments are the primary tool for measuring the causal impact of product changes in digital businesses. It is increasingly common for digital products and services to interact with customers in a personalised way. Using online controlled experiments to optimise personalised interaction strategies is challenging because the usual assumption of statistically equivalent user groups is violated. Additionally, challenges are introduced by users qualifying for strategies based on dynamic, stochastic attributes. Traditional A/B tests can salvage statistical equivalence by pre-allocating users to control and exposed groups, but this dilutes the experimental metrics and reduces the test power. We present a stacked incrementality test framework that addresses problems with running online experiments for personalised user strategies. We derive bounds that show that our framework is superior to the best simple A/B test given enough users and that this condition is easily met for large scale online experiments. In addition, we provide a test power calculator and describe a selection of pitfalls and lessons learnt from our experience using it.

keenable.title: Crowds Believe in You:Online Prediction Markets OverestimateHow Often People Achieve Their Own Goals
keenable.snippet:
Research on the planning fallacy finds that observers predict a person’s behavior less optimistically than the person does, and prediction markets aggregate such judgments, harnessing the wisdom of crowds. We study 6,150 prediction markets on Manifold in which 1,660 users asked about their own futures (“Will I …?”), reconstruct every order and execution, and compare these self-markets with markets about external events. Self-markets resolved YES 4.4 percentage points less often than their final prices implied, whereas external markets were nearly calibrated (0.9 points); the difference was 2.2 points at the same price level and 1.9 points within creators who made both kinds of market. Absent when markets opened, the overstatement emerged within a day of trading, even where the person never traded, and peaked in the week before close. In a market’s first day, observers moved external-market prices down toward the base rate, but moved self-market prices 3.6 points further toward YES, except in markets naming an outcome the person would not want, which were not overpriced. The correction came late and largely from the person, whose orders supplied 38% of the eventual movement toward the outcome in self-markets, against 9% in external markets. Because self-market prices mainly failed to separate successes from failures, a recalibration learned from earlier markets improved later forecasts by only 1.5%.

Lab studies of self- and social prediction cast observers as the corrective to optimistic self-prediction: free of the actor’s plans and hopes, they consult base rates and past behavior [3, 6, 7]. In the markets studied here, observers aggregated through a market and paid for accuracy did not play that role. They brought an outside view to external events, selling prices down toward the rate at which such events occur, but not to the goals people set for themselves, and markets about people ended up overstating those goals.

keenable-realtime.title: Online Controlled Experiments for Personalised e-Commerce Strategies: Design, Challenges, and Pitfalls
keenable-realtime.snippet: Online controlled experiments are the primary tool for measuring the causal impact of product changes in digital businesses. It is increasingly common for digital products and services to interact with customers in a personalised way. Using online controlled experiments to optimise personalised interaction strategies is challenging because the usual assumption of statistically equivalent user groups is violated. Additionally, challenges are introduced by users qualifying for strategies based on dynamic, stochastic attributes. Traditional A/B tests can salvage statistical equivalence by pre-allocating users to control and exposed groups, but this dilutes the experimental metrics and reduces the test power. We present a stacked incrementality test framework that addresses problems with running online experiments for personalised user strategies. We derive bounds that show that our framework is superior to the best simple A/B test given enough users and that this condition is easily met for large scale online experiments. In addition, we provide a test power calculator and describe a selection of pitfalls and lessons learnt from our experience using it.

keenable-realtime.title: Crowds Believe in You:Online Prediction Markets OverestimateHow Often People Achieve Their Own Goals
keenable-realtime.snippet:
Research on the planning fallacy finds that observers predict a person’s behavior less optimistically than the person does, and prediction markets aggregate such judgments, harnessing the wisdom of crowds. We study 6,150 prediction markets on Manifold in which 1,660 users asked about their own futures (“Will I …?”), reconstruct every order and execution, and compare these self-markets with markets about external events. Self-markets resolved YES 4.4 percentage points less often than their final prices implied, whereas external markets were nearly calibrated (0.9 points); the difference was 2.2 points at the same price level and 1.9 points within creators who made both kinds of market. Absent when markets opened, the overstatement emerged within a day of trading, even where the person never traded, and peaked in the week before close. In a market’s first day, observers moved external-market prices down toward the base rate, but moved self-market prices 3.6 points further toward YES, except in markets naming an outcome the person would not want, which were not overpriced. The correction came late and largely from the person, whose orders supplied 38% of the eventual movement toward the outcome in self-markets, against 9% in external markets. Because self-market prices mainly failed to separate successes from failures, a recalibration learned from earlier markets improved later forecasts by only 1.5%.

Lab studies of self- and social prediction cast observers as the corrective to optimistic self-prediction: free of the actor’s plans and hopes, they consult base rates and past behavior [3, 6, 7]. In the markets studied here, observers aggregated through a market and paid for accuracy did not play that role. They brought an outside view to external events, selling prices down toward the rate at which such events occur, but not to the goals people set for themselves, and markets about people ended up overstating those goals.

- Focus  
AI agents acting as shoppers browse or judge a control and one or more variants, and the tool predicts which version would perform better. Some tools drive real browsers on live or staged pages, others compare screenshots. It is a way to pre-screen ideas, not a substitute for a live experiment.

linkup.snippet:
Retailers can use the method to test whether buyers are actually informed, as well as to forecast responses to new information and to calculate how much shoppers would benefit from learning more about a product or service. The researchers tested their model’s predictions in two ways. First, they conducted an experiment in which 196 participants chose one e-book from sets of three randomly selected books sold on Amazon Kindle.
The researchers then varied whether participants could see a randomly assigned discount for each book: For five of the 20 book selections, people could see the discounts without needing to do anything further. For the additional 15 selections, participants had to decide whether to spend a portion of $15 in credits provided to them for each choice. This setup simulated the effort of searching.
The innovation behind the method is technical, but in short, instead of measuring how much customer demand shifts in response to changes in a product feature, the model measures how much the responsiveness itself varies between buyers. This approach allows the researchers to isolate the choices of shoppers who behave as if they are fully informed even when they do not investigate every product.
The model, using only shopper behavior and without examining the website itself, proved able to figure out that the location was initially hidden. While this was a simple test, it indicated that the researchers’ model could be more successful than standard approaches at valuing features such as hotel location.

View PDF HTML (experimental)Abstract:A/B testing is the gold standard for evaluating product changes, but each experiment requires real user traffic, engineering effort, and weeks of measurement. We propose a simulation framework that predicts A/B test outcomes using LLM-powered agents conditioned on data-driven personas grounded in real user behavioral signals. Unlike prior work that relies on synthetic or rule-based personas, our agents are constructed from anonymized behavioral data-activity patterns, engagement signals, and inferred demographics-enabling more faithful population modeling. In the fast-moving digital world, even experts have a hard time assessing new ideas. Case in point: At Bing a small headline change an employee proposed was deemed a low priority and shelved forIn 2012 a Microsoft employee working on Bing had an idea about changing the way the search engine displayed ad headlines. Developing it wouldn’t require much effort—just a few days of an engineer’s time—but it was one of hundreds of ideas proposed, and the program managers deemed it a low priority. So it languished for more than six months, until an engineer, who saw that the cost of writing the code for it would be small, launched a simple online controlled experiment—an A/B test—to assess its impact. Within hours the new headline variation was producing abnormally high revenue, triggering a “too good to be true” alert. Usually, such alerts signal a bug, but not in this case. An analysis showed that the change had increased revenue by an astonishing 12%—which on an annual basis would come to more than $100 million in the United States alone—without hurting key user-experience metrics. It was the best revenue-generating idea in Bing’s history, but until the test its value was underappreciated.

perplexity.title: Squoosh Bench: Insights from 318 Historical A/B Tests
perplexity.snippet:
This research focuses on how experimentation teams can make informed decisions about website changes by utilizing forecasts generated from simulated user behavior.
## Executive Summary
The study analyzed 412 historical A/B tests conducted on websites, narrowing down to 318 tests that lasted longer than 21 days.
The goal was to see if predictions made by different systems about the potential success of website changes could aid in selecting which changes to test in a live environment.
Four forecasting systems were evaluated based on their ability to predict the outcomes of these tests.
The analysis involved masking page roles and withholding recorded outcomes during the prediction phase to ensure unbiased results.
Among the systems tested, Squoosh UX-1, which is specifically fine-tuned using human browsing data, demonstrated a high level of accuracy.
It correctly classified 267 out of 318 test outcomes, achieving an accuracy rate of 84%.
This means that for the experiments where it predicted a win for a new variant, a significant majority of those predictions turned out to be accurate.
In contrast, the Qwen3 Next 80B system, which is recognized for its general-purpose capabilities, had a lower accuracy rate, correctly classifying 196 out of 318 outcomes, or about 62%.
Despite this difference in performance, both systems provided valuable insights into potential website changes.
The research highlighted that UX-1 favored new variants in 126 of the tests it evaluated.
When these variants were subsequently tested live, 93.7% (or 118 out of 126) of the time, the variants that were predicted to perform better actually won.
Only four variants lost, while four results were deemed inconclusive.
This strong correlation between the predictions and actual outcomes suggests that using simulated shopper data can significantly enhance decision-making in web experimentation.

ultimate.title: Online Controlled Experiments for Personalised e-Commerce Strategies: Design, Challenges, and Pitfalls
ultimate.snippet: Online controlled experiments are the primary tool for measuring the causal impact of product changes in digital businesses. It is increasingly common for digital products and services to interact with customers in a personalised way. Using online controlled experiments to optimise personalised interaction strategies is challenging because the usual assumption of statistically equivalent user groups is violated. Additionally, challenges are introduced by users qualifying for strategies based on dynamic, stochastic attributes. Traditional A/B tests can salvage statistical equivalence by pre-allocating users to control and exposed groups, but this dilutes the experimental metrics and reduces the test power. We present a stacked incrementality test framework that addresses problems with running online experiments for personalised user strategies. We derive bounds that show that our framework is superior to the best simple A/B test given enough users and that this condition is easily met for large scale online experiments. In addition, we provide a test power calculator and describe a selection of pitfalls and lessons learnt from our experience using it.

ultimate.title: Crowds Believe in You:Online Prediction Markets OverestimateHow Often People Achieve Their Own Goals
ultimate.snippet:
Research on the planning fallacy finds that observers predict a person’s behavior less optimistically than the person does, and prediction markets aggregate such judgments, harnessing the wisdom of crowds. We study 6,150 prediction markets on Manifold in which 1,660 users asked about their own futures (“Will I …?”), reconstruct every order and execution, and compare these self-markets with markets about external events. Self-markets resolved YES 4.4 percentage points less often than their final prices implied, whereas external markets were nearly calibrated (0.9 points); the difference was 2.2 points at the same price level and 1.9 points within creators who made both kinds of market. Absent when markets opened, the overstatement emerged within a day of trading, even where the person never traded, and peaked in the week before close. In a market’s first day, observers moved external-market prices down toward the base rate, but moved self-market prices 3.6 points further toward YES, except in markets naming an outcome the person would not want, which were not overpriced. The correction came late and largely from the person, whose orders supplied 38% of the eventual movement toward the outcome in self-markets, against 9% in external markets. Because self-market prices mainly failed to separate successes from failures, a recalibration learned from earlier markets improved later forecasts by only 1.5%.

Lab studies of self- and social prediction cast observers as the corrective to optimistic self-prediction: free of the actor’s plans and hopes, they consult base rates and past behavior [3, 6, 7]. In the markets studied here, observers aggregated through a market and paid for accuracy did not play that role. They brought an outside view to external events, selling prices down toward the rate at which such events occur, but not to the goals people set for themselves, and markets about people ended up overstating those goals.

ultimate.title: Predicting Field Experiments with Large Language Models
ultimate.snippet:
Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated unprecedented emergent capabilities, including content generation, translation, and simulation of human behavior. Field experiments, on the other hand, are widely employed in social studies to examine real-world human behavior through carefully designed manipulations and treatments. However, field experiments are known to be expensive and time consuming. Therefore, an interesting question is whether and how LLMs can be utilized for field experiments. In this paper, we propose and evaluate an automated LLM-based framework to predict the outcomes of a field experiment. Applying this framework to 276 experiments about a wide range of human behaviors drawn from renowned economics literature yields a prediction accuracy of 78%. Moreover, we find that the distributions of the results are either bimodal or highly skewed. By investigating this abnormality further, we identify that field experiments related to complex social issues such as ethnicity, social norms, and ethical dilemmas can pose significant challenges to the prediction performance.

In this paper, we fill the literature gap by proposing an automated LLM framework to predict the outcome of a wide range of field experiments.

We test this framework on 276 field experiments reported in premier academic journals from 2000 to 2024. Those experiments contain a total of 1261 conclusions with a wide range of topics such as labor-market discrimination, educational incentives, household finance behavior, and the impact of healthcare enrollment. Without any alignment techniques or fine-tuning, our framework achieves an average prediction accuracy of 78%.

For homepages, both explanations are probably true simultaneously. The root cause of homepage testing's poor performance is not mysterious once you understand the psychology. Homepages suffer from what you might call the audience fragmentation problem: they serve too many people with too many different needs at the same time.
It needs to route people toward the right downstream experience based on their intent. No single change to a homepage can optimize for all of these audiences simultaneously. When you make the hero section more compelling for new visitors, you may slow down returning users who just want to navigate to their account. This is a direct application of what Herbert Simon called satisficing -- in complex environments with multiple competing objectives, you cannot optimize; you can only find acceptable compromises.
